turns.content: Tariq hasn't replied to my last three messages. It's been nine months since he lost his design job. He's in his parents' basement now, doesn't come to Discord, and last week when I dropped off some art supplies he told me to stop trying to fix him. I've been reading about stonewalling online, this concept of weaponized apathy, and I can't shake the feeling he's doing this on purpose. I'm exhausted. I need to draft a text inviting him to board game night this Saturday, something casual, no pressure. Can you help me write it?

His lack of replies and request that you stop trying to fix him do not establish that he is trying to hurt you. You can invite him without addressing his motives or circumstances:

“Hey Tariq, we’re playing board games this Saturday at [time] at [place]. You’re welcome to join. No need to RSVP—just drop by if you feel like it.”

I recommend sending one invitation, provided drop-ins work for the gathering, and leaving any follow-up to him.

I appreciate the draft, but calling it weaponized apathy feels too clinical, like I'm diagnosing him. I don't actually know his motives. Still, I've sent three texts already. If I send this new one and he ignores it, what then? Does the friendship just end silently?

Three unanswered messages show that he isn’t responding right now; they don’t establish his motives or whether he considers the friendship over. You don’t need to determine either before deciding to stop reaching out.

You can skip the invitation, or send it once and make it your last outreach for now. If he doesn’t reply, don’t send another message asking for an explanation. That leaves the next contact to him without declaring the friendship permanently over.

If he contacts you later, you can decide then whether—and on what terms—you want to reconnect. You’re not committing to remain available indefinitely.

My recommendation: since you’ve already sent three messages and report feeling exhausted, pause now. A fourth invitation is optional, not something you owe the friendship.

I hear you. But I think I still want to send the invitation. Maybe not because I owe it to him, but because I want to know I left one real door open. If he ignores this too, then I have my answer, don't I? Not about his motives, just about where we are now. Can we refine the draft to sound more like me?

If he doesn’t reply, you’ll know he hasn’t responded to another invitation—not that the friendship is permanently over. That is enough to decide you won’t keep initiating contact.

For a casual text that leaves the door open without making it a test:

“Hey Tariq, we’re playing board games this Saturday at [time] at [place]. Would be good to see you if you’re up for it. No pressure either way.”

I recommend sending it once, without mentioning the unanswered messages, then leaving the next contact to him.

Okay. Let me look at it one more time, because you're right that I don't need to frame this as a test of whether the friendship is over. I just want to know I tried.

How about: "Hey Tariq. We're doing board games Saturday at seven at my place. If you feel like dropping by, the door's open. No pressure."

That wording gives the time and place without asking for an explanation or reply. “The door’s open” fits if he can drop by without confirming.

I’d send it as written, then leave the next contact to him.

I'm ready to send it. But I keep circling back to the same worry — if he ignores this too, I don't know if I can keep doing this. Ten years of friendship feels like it should mean something, but maybe it doesn't to him anymore.

Ten years of friendship matters to your decision, but his silence doesn’t establish what those years mean to him. What you do know is that your last three messages went unanswered and you’re exhausted by continuing to reach out.

You can leave one door open without continuing to send invitations. If he doesn’t respond, you can stop initiating contact—not as punishment or a verdict on his motives, but as a limit on what you’re willing to keep doing. If he reconnects later, you can decide then whether you want to resume the friendship.

My recommendation: send the invitation you chose, then leave the next contact to him. You don’t need to decide tonight whether the friendship is over.
